articles.text: Coalition of U.S. cities fighting for right to limit cell towers The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals’ decision in City of Portland v. United States (2020) significantly affects the ability of local governments to regulate the installation of “small cell” wireless facilities. On March 22, Piedmont joined a national coalition of dozens of cities, led by the City of Portland, to file a writ of certiorari to review the judgement of the Court of Appeals. A writ of certiorari is a request that the Supreme Court order a lower court to send up the record of the case for review. The Supreme Court decision is currently pending. The Federal Communication Commission issued the Third Order, or “Carr Order,” in September 2018, which limited Piedmont’s control over the applications filed by Crown Castle LLC in 2017 and 2019. Crown Castle first applied for Wireless Communications Facilities Permits (WCF Permits) in October of 2016. When Piedmont turned down an application by Crown Castle for cell towers, the company sued the city. In August 2020 the Ninth Circuit Court upheld most of the provisions of the Carr Order. The City of Piedmont filed an appeal of the order in federal court, citing that it was without precedent. Piedmont joined a coalition of much larger cities, including Atlanta, Boston, Philadelphia, Chicago, Los Angeles, San Jose, Santa Monica, and Monterey. The Federal Communication Commission (FCC) and the United States of America are the respondents in the court case. The consortium of cities is being represented by Best, Best & Krieger LLP, a law firm based in Walnut Creek. The firm maintains a strong presence in Washington, D.C., where lawyers regularly meet with key members of the FCC as well as members of Congress on issues related to telecommunications. The firm’s area of expertise includes cell tower siting, wireless communications, and interplay of federal and state regulations, among others. Firm partner Gerry Lederer participated in a recorded debate on 5G and its impact on cities’ right of way, as well as the challenges posed by ongoing conflicts between the wireless industry and local government agencies, and said that “the FCC has tilted the table too much in favor of industry and not enough for communities.” “It would be nice if industry would tell the truth about size. Small cells are not ‘small’. [They should] stop going to state legislatures and city councils with small boxes and saying ‘this is a small cell’, and forgetting about the other 28 cubic feet that [come along with it,]” he said. More information about the case is available at: https://www. supremecourt.gov/search.aspx- ?filename=/docket/DocketFiles/ html/Public/20-1354.html.

articles.text: Editor: We now know the elementary school day schedule will remain unchanged through June. Our youngest learners will see their teachers in-person for only 9 hours a week, instead of the 30 in-person hours a week offered by comparable, Bay Area school districts. In a letter to elementary school families, Superintendent Booker wrote that not adding more in-person instructional minutes “... may be a disappointment to some community members.” Let’s consider that “some” is actually “most” and “community members” are the “students we strive to serve,” especially since at this point, there is no scientific or safety restriction preventing every student from being in-person at school full-time. Our inability to move past these logistics is reflective of the results of the recent communication survey that demonstrated that both teachers and families alike don’t trust our leadership to hold our interests at heart. On May 5, 2021, the school board held a special closed-door session to review Superintendent Booker’s performance and to discuss the upcoming teacher negotiations. Despite many pleas for greater transparency from families, the board returned after the closed session to announce “no action was taken.” No further details were provided. And so, where do we go from here? After the challenges of this year, each group of stakeholders needs to ask themselves a series of questions: • Do you respect and look toward our superintendent, assistant superintendent and school board for honest leadership and expertise? • Would new leadership at all levels be the most efficient way forward? School board members should be asking themselves: • Can you effectively and objectively evaluate our superintendent and assistant superintendent? • Have you provided clear and consistent direction for the district with the wellbeing of the students at the center, guiding your decisions?
articles.title: Piedmont is behind. Here’s how we can move ahead

articles.text: Experts predict an early wildfire season due to dry conditions On May 10, Gov. Gavin Newsom added 39 counties to the state’s emergency drought proclamation, which include Alameda County and three others in the Bay Area. Alameda, Contra Costa, Napa and Solano counties were added to the proclamation. Newsom has proposed a $5.1 billion investment in water infrastructure and drought resilience in the state budget as California is confronted with critical water shortages. The allocation includes $1.3 billion for drinking and wastewater infrastructure, $60 million to assist the agriculture industry in reducing its water use and greenhouse gas emissions, and $200 million for habitat restoration. “This package of bold investments will equip the state with the tools we need to tackle the drought emergency head-on while addressing long-standing water challenges,” Gov. Newsom said. The 41 counties now under a drought state of emergency represents 30 percent of the state’s population. The state issued a “red flag” fire warning on May 2, the first time a red flag warning was issued in May since 2014. Red flag warnings are triggered by a combination of dry, hot conditions and strong winds. While temperatures around the Bay Area in the last week, have been unseasonably cold, when the warning was issued, temperatures were about 15 degrees Fahrenheit above average temperatures. EBMUD makes it official; drought is here The Board of Directors at East Bay Municipal Utility District, or EBMUD, voted to declare a Stage 1 drought shortage at its April 27 meeting based on projections that water runoff will fall below what is needed to refill reservoirs this year. The board also voted to purchase supplemental water supplies from the Sacramento River at the same meeting. The utility district, which serves Piedmont residents, has asked customers to Map courtesy of the Drought Monitor (https://droughtmonitor.unl.edu/) Most of California including the Bay Area is in “Extreme” or “Exceptional” Drought. begin voluntary conservation to save water supplies now. “This year has been the second driest year on record in our Mokelumne River watershed and the driest year on record in the East Bay,” Board President Doug Linney said. “Fortunately, we started last year well, and our customers continued saving water in our drought-prone region. However, we must take initial actions now to ensure we don’t face harder choices next year.” EBMUD is asking customers to observe water use regulations, which include: checking and repairing leaks in toilets and irrigation systems, prohibiting the use of potable water for construction, street cleaning or dust control where an alternative recycled source is available, and adjusting outdoor irrigation timers or manually water landscapes three times a week or less and at dawn or dusk to avoid evaporation. Rate increase proposed by EBMUD Mandatory restrictions are not currently in place, nor are drought surcharges; however, EDMUD is proposing to increase the rates for both its water and wastewater service charges based on its most recent rate models and cost of service studies. Rates would increase over a two-year period, by approximately 4 percent overall on July 1, 2021, followed by another 4 percent increase the next year, July 1, 2022. This is an approximate increase, individual bills may increase by slightly more or less that amount depending on the specific rates and charges that apply to you and how much water you use. EBMUD will hold a public hearing on the proposed rate increase on Tuesday, June 8, at 1:15 p.m. It will be conducted via Zoom. The public may participate in the hearing virtual or by telephone. The Zoom Meeting ID is 958-6681-4531, and passcode is 810650. You must enter both when you participate in the meeting telephonically (by calling 1-699-900-6833) or virtually (by visiting www.edmud.com/rates.) Written comments may be mailed before the hearing date to EDMUD, MS 218, PO Box 24055, Oakland, CA 94623-1055. Fire season’s grim outlook The length of fire season is estimated to be 2-1/2 months longer this year across the Sierras and throughout the state, according to Cal Fire, the California Department of Forestry and Fire Prevention. It cites climate change as the main cause of prolonged wildfire seasons. Warmer spring and summer temperatures and reduced snowpack create longer dry seasons.

articles.text: On August 28, 1963, people gathered in Washington, D.C. to hear this powerful declaration: “I have a dream that my four little children will one day live in a nation where they will not be judged by the color of their skin, but by the content of their character.” This was beautifully spoken by Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. I am beyond sadden that society today is tearing apart Dr. King’s work that he painstakingly fought for. Dr. King’s legacy is being torn down by people who are demanding that you recognize your skin color as a determinate of your character. If you are White you are the oppressor; if you are non-White you are Recently President Biden and Vice President Kamala Harris agreed with South Carolina Senator Tim Scott (the only Black Republican in the U.S. Senate) that the U.S. is not a racist country. Yet, throughout the U.S., school districts are contemplating the implementation of Critical Race Theory (CRT) to their The basic ideological beliefs include “Whiteness” as oppression and propagation of racial stereotypes that the way people think and act are tied to their skin color. Decades ago in the segregated South, the emphasis upon skin color was deemed racist, but in today’s modern society, this is viewed as a progressive way of battling racism. The USA is the land of the free, the land of opportunity. This is the land that my ancestors fled to in order to feed their starving families left behind in their native land; this is the land that my ancestors fought to travel to and from during the Chinese Exclusion Act; this is the land that contained my ancestors on Angel Island; this is the land that my ancestors escaped to from Chinese Communist control; this is the land where my ancestors faced discrimination. And this is the land that I hold dear to my heart because of the freedom and opportunities that have been afforded to my ancestors, myself and, hopefully, to the next generations to come based on hard work and character – and not on race. As a parent I must do what I can to protect and educate my children. In today’s turbulent times, it is difficult for individuals to openly express their dissatisfaction with the mainstream. There is fear of being censured, ostracized, categorized a racist or sell-out when going against the tide. pages.text: Wednesday, May 19, 2021 3 Alameda County added to drought emergency list Experts predict an early wildfire season due to dry conditions By Allyson Aleksey On May 10, Gov. Gavin Newsom added 39 counties to the state’s emergency drought proclamation, which include Alameda County and three others in the Bay Area. Alameda, Contra Costa, Napa and Solano counties were added to the proclamation. Newsom has proposed a $5.1 billion investment in water infrastructure and drought resilience in the state budget as California is confronted with critical water shortages. The allocation includes $1.3 billion for drinking and wastewater infrastructure, $60 million to assist the agriculture industry in reducing its water use and greenhouse gas emissions, and $200 million for habitat restoration. “This package of bold investments will equip the state with the tools we need to tackle the drought emergency head-on while addressing long-standing water challenges,” Gov. Newsom said. The 41 counties now under a drought state of emergency represents 30 percent of the state’s population. The state issued a “red flag” fire warning on May 2, the first time a red flag warning was issued in May since 2014. Red flag warnings are triggered by a combination of dry, hot conditions and strong winds. While temperatures around the Bay Area in the last week, have been unseasonably cold, when the warning was issued, temperatures were about 15 degrees Fahrenheit above average temperatures. EBMUD makes it official; drought is here The Board of Directors at East Bay Municipal Utility District, or EBMUD, voted to declare a Stage 1 drought shortage at its April 27 meeting based on projections that water runoff will fall below what is needed to refill reservoirs this year. The board also voted to purchase supplemental water supplies from the Sacramento River at the same meeting. The utility district, which serves Piedmont residents, has asked customers to Map courtesy of the Drought Monitor (https://droughtmonitor.unl.edu/) Most of California including the Bay Area is in “Extreme” or “Exceptional” Drought. begin voluntary conservation to save water supplies now. “This year has been the second driest year on record in our Mokelumne River watershed and the driest year on record in the East Bay,” Board President Doug Linney said. “Fortunately, we started last year well, and our customers continued saving water in our drought-prone region. However, we must take initial actions now to ensure we don’t face harder choices next year.” EBMUD is asking customers to observe water use regulations, which include: checking and repairing leaks in toilets and irrigation systems, prohibiting the use of potable water for construction, street cleaning or dust control where an alternative recycled source is available, and adjusting outdoor irrigation timers or manually water landscapes three times a week or less and at dawn or dusk to avoid evaporation. Rate increase proposed by EBMUD Mandatory restrictions are not currently in place, nor are drought surcharges; however, EDMUD is proposing to increase the rates for both its water and wastewater service charges based on its most recent rate models and cost of service studies. This is an approximate increase, individual bills may increase by slightly more or less that amount depending on the specific rates and charges that apply to you and how much water you use. articles.text: Ordinance 750 N.S., or “reach codes,” will go into effect on Tuesday, June 1. The amendment was adopted by Piedmont’s City Council on February 1 and will affect sales and transfers of real estate and the construction of new and existing residential buildings. Reach codes require certain home renovation projects to include energy efficiency measures or photovoltaic systems. For renovation projects that cost more than $25,000, at least one from a series of energy efficiency measures must be included in the project. For renovations costing more than $100,000, two energy efficient measures must be included. It is up to the homeowner which option or options to choose. Options range from less expensive options, such as switching out lightbulbs, to more expensive ones, like replacing water heaters. For reference, in 2019, 22% of building permits had a cost over $25,000, and 5% of building permits had a cost over $100,000. But more than threefourths of all projects had a value under $25,000 and would not be affected by these requirements. All new homes constructed in Piedmont, including new detached Accessory Dwelling Units (ADUs), will be prohibited from having natural gas supplied to them. Building a new, all-electric home is expected to be less expensive than one with gas. Installing a new gas line can cost thousands of dollars, which all-electric homes will not need. Ordinance 750 N.S. was approved by the California Energy Commission on May 12. The ordinance is intended to reduce greenhouse gas emissions stemming from natural gas appliances. In staff reports related to the adoption of reach codes, city council found that “increasing levels of atmospheric greenhouse gas concentrates are expected to result in global temperature increases, and based on scientific literature and studies, are likely to cause a variety of local changes, including extreme weather conditions, sea level rise, more frequent heat waves, and extended period of drought.” We are currently feeling the effects of extreme weather caused by greenhouse gas concentrates. As more emissions enter the atmosphere, there is less precipitation and higher temperatures across California, leading to an increased likelihood of fires and drought. Even though Piedmont is small, it has the highest per capita emissions in the entire Bay Area, meaning that each citizen of Piedmont emits more greenhouse gases than average citizens anywhere else in the Bay. The majority of these emissions come from natural gas appliances. Home Energy Score (Home Energy Audit) Additionally, Ordinance 751 N.S., or the home energy assessment policy, went into effect on March 3 and affects homeowners and real estate agents. When selling a property or transferring the title, the seller must provide potential buyers with a Home Energy Score or Home Energy Audit prepared in the past five years, in addition to the normal disclosure information. Getting a Home Energy Score involves a few simple steps that can be accomplished while still living in the home. You can schedule a home energy assessment by contacting an authorized Home Energy Assessor before listing, or otherwise announcing your home for sale. The City maintains a list of authorized Assessors on its site: (https://piedmont.ca.gov/cms/ one.aspx?portalId=13659823&p ageId=17415806). Assessors also can be found by a Google search. Once you choose an assessment company, a Home Energy Assessor will visit your home to assess it. They will collect information about a home’s foundation, insulation, walls, and windows, as well as its heating, cooling, and water systems. CEC’s new Energy Code Draft Every three years, the California Energy Commission (CEC) approves a new Energy Code, which impacts how structures are built and renovated during that code cycle. Two weeks ago, the CEC released their proposed changes to the 2022 Energy Code, to take effect January 1, 2023. This is what’s called the “45-day language”, meaning that everyone has 45 days to review and provide comments, which are due June 21, 2021. If members of Piedmont want to comment on the proposed Energy Code, they can send them to the website: (https://efiling.energy.ca.gov/EComment/ EComment.aspx?docketnumber=21-BSTD-01). There will be three public hearings available on Zoom on May 24, 27, and 28. The Energy Code helps dictate the work that the Planning and Building Department completes in Piedmont. For instance, the reach codes came to pass because they “reach” above and beyond the minimum requirements in the Energy Code. The new Code will go into effect in 2023. For any questions about these ordinances, please visit the city’s website at: https:// piedmont.ca.gov/cms/one.aspx? portalId=13659823&pageId= 17415806 or email adykman@ piedmont.ca.gov or nredinbo@ piedmont.ca.gov.
articles.title: Energy Reach Code goes into effect June 1

articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Department has revamped its summer camp and classes, to include bringing back its popular Counselor-In-Training (CIT) program for tweens and teens. articles.text: The pandemic did not stop the Highlander Robotics team from building world-class robots. Their efforts paid off at the Northern California FIRST Robotics Competition (FRC) awards show on Saturday, May 15. The team won the Rookie Game Changer Award for their robot Whirlpool. The Highlanders competed against teams from Australia, India, Norway, Canada, plus teams from all over the U.S. This was a highly unusual and challenging robotics season due to Covid. Instead of competing in person at UC Davis or San Jose State, the team submitted photos and videos of Whirlpool performing various skills challenges. They also interviewed with judges around the world. The team was fortunate to still have access to the Lambert workshop on Dracena Avenue. Piedmont School District offered critical support, letting the team test their software code, practice driving Whirlpool, and film the virtual skills challenges in the Morrison Gym. The Highlanders were very ambitious this season and built an advanced robot. Team member Charlie Lambert advocated for the team to switch to a swerve drivetrain which allows the robot to spin while traveling along any path. It also makes it very easy for the driver to maneuver while still having good traction for defense. Veteran teams warned the Highlanders that the software was extremely complicated and not suitable for a rookie team. Undaunted, software team members Sebastien Combes and Jasper Zietlow got the job done with guidance of mentor Kevin Clark. Whirlpool features a shooter, which launches dodgeballs into an 8-foot tall target, and an innovative climbing mechHighland Robotics Team Photo. Whirlpool, the 2021 Robot. Assembling Whirlpool. Climber team (Alyssa Angsupanich, Basia Young and Alex Ware) with Piedmont resident mentor Klaus Zietlow working on a prototype of the climbing mechanism. Shooter team (Peter Stokes, Will Shields and Reece Beck) gets training on fabricating aluminum on the CNC Router with mentor, John Lambert. Whirlpool’s climbing mechanism in action. anism. Senior Will Shields led the shooter hardware team while Avery Chan and Robbie Sylvia wrote the software that allows it to shoot rapidly and accurately. Alyssa Angsupanich led the team that built Whirlpool’s climbing mechanism. The 100 plus pound robot sports a carbon fiber hook on an extendible cable track and uses a winch to pull itself off the ground. Piedmont resident software mentor, Kevin Clark, juggles questions from software team members virtually and in person. Jasper Zietlow, Sebastien Combes and Henry Lambert working on the code for swerve drive. John Lambert, the team’s fabrication mentor said, “The team made huge strides in the design process this season. Each subteam designed their mechanism in Solidworks (industry leading computer aided design software) and fit them together before any final parts were fabricated. The lab’s new laser cutter was also a huge benefit for prototyping mechanisms.” The Highlanders aim to become a world class team at Piedmont High School. Students and parents interested in getting involved by mentoring, sponsoring, or joining the team, are asked to contact frc8033@piedmontmakers.org. The team is sponsored by NASA, Zenni, Google, Apple, East Bay Community Energy and the Silicon Valley Community Foundation.

articles.text: Morgan Fjord, the Piedmont District Executive (Program Coordinator) has accepted a promotion with the Golden Gate Area Scout Council as District Director, effective May 16. He has served the Piedmont community through Scouting for the past 2½ years. “Morgan has consistently shown dedication and care while working with our Scouting volunteers and youth,” said Scout Executive Kate Benson. “The past year and half in particular have been challenging, with in-person activities disrupted by COVID-19. We’re proud of the work he’s done and wish him the best as he takes the next step in his career.” In his new role, Fjord will be managing one staff member and supporting the Scouting programs in the city and county of San Francisco. “It has been a pleasure working with all of you over the past two years,” said Fjord. “This past year has been tough for us all, but I am proud that we have weathered the worst of it together and have come out strong and ready for this Summer and Fall. “I could list everyone who has helped to make this a reality, but it would be too long. Thank you for the opportunity to work with you all in building the Scouting program in Piedmont. The Piedmont Council Boy Scouts of America serves youth from Kindergarten to age 20 with programs that focus on developing character, fitness, citizenship, and leadership. articles.text: California’s health officers announced on Monday, May 17 that the state’s mask mandate will remain in place until June 15 after the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention put out guidance last week saying people vaccinated against COVID-19 do not have to wear masks inside in most situations. The CDC on Thursday, May 13 said that fully vaccinated Americans can go maskless and without social distancing indoors and outdoors in most cases. The CDC said that masks are only required for the vaccinated in certain instances, like on airplanes or buses. Masking guidelines are ultimately up to local and state governments, the CDC said. After discussing the issue for several days, California made the decision to continue its mask mandate until June 15. “This four-week period will give Californians time to prepare for this change while we continue the relentless focus on delivering vaccines, particularly to underserved communities and those that were hard hit throughout this pandemic,” Health and Human Services Secretary Mark Ghaly said on call with reporters. The CDC’s mask announcement came as a surprise to many across the nation, although several states began adopting the new guidelines within days of the announcement. Many national retailers have announced they will follow the CDC’s plan, although California’s guidelines would supersede any business’ policy. Gov. Gavin Newsom’s office said that the June 15 deadline would allows Californians to prepare for the mask rule change as well as increase the number of vaccinated residents. The state’s mask mandate last changed on May 3, when California adopted CDC guidance that that said fully vaccinated people do not need to wear masks outdoors unless they are in a crowd of strangers. People are considered fully vaccinated if it has been two weeks since either their second dose of Pfizer or Moderna vaccine or their one dose of Johnson & Johnson vaccine. As of Monday, May 18, the rolling seven-day COVID-19 positivity rate in Alameda County is now 1 percent, the lowest point since the pandemic began in March of 2020. Alameda County has yet to meet state benchmarks to move into a less-restrictive tier for reopening its economy, but metrics continue to movie in the right direction. Since March 30, Alameda County has been in the orange tier, or moderate tier, the second-least restrictive tier in California’s color-coded four-tier system. Yesterday, Tuesday, May 18, Santa Clara and Santa Cruz counties joined San Francisco and San Mateo counties in the least-restrictive yellow tier. All other Bay Area counties are in the orange tier, besides Solano County, which has remained in the red tier, or substantial tier, for weeks. Most indoor activities can resume, with modification, in the yellow tier. To move into the yellow tier, the positivity rate in Alameda County needs to stay below 2 percent. The positivity rate in census-designated low-income areas also needs to stay below 2.2 percent – it is currently 1.6 percent in Alameda County. The number of cases per 100,000 people needs to be below 1 – right now there are 2.9 cases per 100,000. The entire color tier system will end the same day as the mask mandate for vaccinated Californians. Newsom announced plans several weeks ago to lift most COVID-19 restrictions statewide on June 15. It is expected that the reopening plan will continue if hospitalizations remain low and vaccination supply is not majorly disrupted. One new case of COVID-19 was reported in Piedmont across the past seven days. The total number of Piedmont cases since the pandemic began is 182. Across Alameda County, the total caseload is 88,157. There have been 27,459 cases recorded in Oakland and 13,670 cases in Hayward. Tragically, the total number of COVID-19 fatalities countywide is now 1,668. As of press time, the California Department of Public Health reported that there have been 3,666,591 total cases of COVID- 19 in California. There have been 61,513 deaths due to the disease statewide. The state positivity rate is 0.9 percent, a record low for the pandemic.

articles.text: Alameda County’s entry into the least restrictive Yellow Tier in the state’s blueprint for re-opening would mean loosened restrictions for music and performance venue operations and live entertainment. While Alameda County has yet to meet benchmarks to move into the Yellow Tier, metrics are currently moving in the right direction to do so. The county has been in the Orange Tier since March 30. To move into the least restrictive, or minimal “yellow tier,” positivity rates in the county need to stay below 2%. Yellow Tier restrictions would vary greatly depending on whether the event is held at an outdoor or indoor venue. Live events are permissible now in the Orange Tier, both in outdoor and indoor venues with restrictions. Indoor venues with a 1,500 capacity can open with a maximum of 25% or 300 people, or 50% if all guests provide proof of full vaccination or show a negative test result within 72 hours prior to attendance. For venues larger than 1,500 seats, there is a 2,000-person capacity, and no eating or drinking is allowed. The capacity goes up to 50% if all guests show proof of full vaccination or a negative test result within 72 hours prior to the event. An indoor venue’s capacity can go up with proof of negative test or vaccination card, but there is no current guideline that says an outdoor venue can increase capacity with proof of vaccination. However, for outdoor venues, according to the California Department of Public Health, only in-state spectators may be allowed; at the time a guest purchases tickets, the operator must obtain an attestation that the guest’s block of seat reservations contains no more than three households and that the guest, and all members of the guest’s party are “in-state visitors.” In April, the East Bay Venue Coalition, Oakland’s Cultural Affairs Commission, and the Alameda County Public Health Department (ACPHD) hosted a virtual town hall meeting to discuss health and safety guidelines for in-person events. While county public health officials can allow for loosened restrictions regardless of state-wide status, the County Public Health Department has confirmed that it will be following the state’s “Blueprint for a Safer Economy,” which provides specific guidelines for industries, including the live entertainment industry. Note that, current rules are temporary and will not apply after June 15 if vaccine supply is sufficient and hospitalization rates remain low. Gov. Gavin Newsom said that California will move away from its color-coded tier system, and Blueprint for a Safer Economy, by that date. There are currently no county-wide rules for what venues and event organizers will be required to do after June 15.

Max Wagener added two goals to make it 7-0 before the Trojans’ first score with 58 seconds left in the first half. Peter Krumins made the game 8-1 at halftime. Piedmont added goals from Davis, Wagener, and Sam Corcoran in the third quarter, 11-3. With Stein and Wagener resting the fourth quarter, PHS gained scores from Dunlap, two from Jake Hart, Antonio Rivera, Krumins, and George Stein. Final stats: Stein with five goals and one steal. But Piedmont burst open the lead with a huge third quarter for a 14-8 lead, then tacked on four goals in the last quarter for the 18-12 final. Wagener scored to make it 3-3 at the end of the first. After trailing 6-4, Piedmont tied it at 6-6 with scores from Dunlap and Hart. Alhambra went ahead 7-6 in the third quarter, but four unanswered goals by Miller and Wagener, two each, put the Highlanders in the lead to stay at 10-7. articles.text: PHS water polo players are encouraged by their coach. The PHS girls’ water polo team had a thrilling group of matches last week, beating Berkeley 10-5 on Thursday, May 13, followed by a close 6-3 loss against Alhambra in Martinez on Monday, May 17, and a razorthin 7-6 loss last night to Castro Valley. “It was an exciting win against Berkeley. We pulled ourselves together late in the games against Alhambra and Castro Valley after allowing some early goals,” said coach Sarah Mooney. The Berkeley win featured Piedmont’s hole set Ella Wright scoring five goals. She also scored three against Castro Valley. Big win vs. Berkeley, 9-3 Piedmont led 3-2 by the end of the first quarter, jumped ahead 5-2 by halftime and put the game out of reach at 9-3 by the end of the third period. Wright opened the scoring with two goals in the first six minutes. Macie Gard made it 3-0 with 4:40 left in the first, but Berkeley scored twice to close the gap to 3-2 after the first period. Annika Nilsson scored two minutes into the 2nd quarter and Odessa Dando boosted Piedmont’s lead to 5-2 with 3:14 before halftime. The Highlanders added three more goals in the third quarter, from Gard with 5:53 left, Wright after a quick steal 30 seconds later, and another goal with 3:50 remaining in the third. After a Yellowjackets’ goal, Wright rocketed in her fifth and final goal, 9-3. Nillson scored Piedmont’s last goal with 6:37 left in the game, making it 10-3 before the Jackets’ tacked on two late goals for the 10-5 final. Final stats: Wright’s five goals, five ejections drawn, and one steal. Nillson had two goals, one assist and three steals. Gard also scored twice with one assist and a steal. 6-3 loss to Alhambra The Highlanders trailed 3-0 after the first three minutes but fought back to a 4-3 deficit by the start of the fourth quarter. However, the Highlanders were not able to find the goal another time in the later going. Frankie Broening, Dando and Nilsson were the goal scorers, official times were not recorded. One-goal loss to Castro Valley The Highlanders battled to a 7-6 loss against Castro Valley last night, May 18, after battling back from a 5-1 deficit at halftime. In fact, Piedmont took a 6-5 lead heading into the fourth quarter, but couldn’t sustain the advantage. Wright’s goal in the first quarter made it a 3-1 game. The Trojans tacked on two more goals in the second quarter before the Highlanders rallied for a 6-5 left with 22 seconds left in the third period. The comeback started with a Broening goal with 5:08 left in the third quarter, followed by Wright with 4:20 to go. Gard scored two minutes later and Gwen Jones tied it with 1:50 left in the quarter. With 22 seconds left in the third quarter, Wright put PHS ahead 6-5. Final stats: Wright with three goals; Broening, Gard, and Jones had individual goals. NEXT UP Piedmont (2-3) heads to San Leandro tomorrow, Thursday, May 20 for a 4:30 p.m. match. The Highlanders then compete in the season-ending WACC League Tournament at Encinal on Tuesday, May 25. articles.text: The Tule Elk State Natural Reserve can be found north of Tomales Bay State Park and the small town of Inverness by Pt. Reyes National Seashore. A High Surf Advisory along the California coast made for terrific wave-watching, and the near-five mile hike to Tomales Point put walkers next to herds of Tule Elk completely undisturbed by passersby. Taking the 9.7 mile out-andback Tomales Point Trail heads to the northern most point on the Inverness side of Tomales Bay – overlooking remote stretches of beaches on the Pacific to the south and Dillon Beach to the north. The hike starts at Pierce Point Two bulls rest, posing perfectly for the shot. A young spike grazes near the trail, undisturbed by hikers. The view toward Tomales Point during January’s High Surf Advisory. Ranch, a historic farmstead of the Pt. Reyes Peninsula that has informative markers to describe the early dairy farming culture of the area. The walk to Tomales Point is in conjunction with the Tule Elk Reserve, where herds of male bulls, female cows, young male spikes, and baby calves. The trail ends at a bluff overlooking tidepools and an array of pelicans, cormorants, gulls, while redtailed hawks and turkey vultures. The main attraction, the Tule Elk, are native to Central California and regarded as the smallest subspecies of elk. They were a big part of Pt. Reyes becoming a National Seashore in 1976. At that time, the species faced local extinction due to hunting in the 1850s. In the fall of 1978, the National Park Service released 17 elk into the area after converting decommissioned farmland into a reserve. Now the park has over 400 elk. The area is located along the wind-swept region of Bodega Bay on the ridgeline of the Pt. Reyes National Seashore. Without any tree coverage, visitors should wear proper attire given they can experience high-winds, fog, and rain at any random moment. Although officially considered a 9.7 mile, mostly flat round-trip, our odometer came out at 10.45 miles and an elevation gain of 1,336 feet. To locate this hike, punch in “Tomales Point Trailhead” or “Pierce Point Ranch” to your GPS device. Originally published in the Post on January 13, 2021.
articles.title: Tule Elk, Tomales Point, & Pt. Reyes Seashore

The University of California, Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive (BAMPFA) is offering a look at the effects of colonialism on Latin American and Caribbean arts in a new exhibition entitled “Present Tense: Five Centuries of Colonialism.” “Present Tense” examines both historical and contemporary works that reveal how colonization has shaped life in the Latin Americas and Caribbean islands. The artists in this exhibition have experienced lingering injustices in the wake of colonialism. The exhibition was organized by History of Art Professor Todd Olson and Associate Professor of Spanish and Portuguese Ivonne del Valle. It is the fifth in a series of annual exhibitions called “Cal Conversations”. developed in collaboration with UC Berkeley classes. The exhibition opened on April 30, and will be open through June 20. To obtain timed tickets, visit https://bampfa.org/program/ virtual/present-tense-five-centuries-colonialism-latin-american-and-caribbean-art.

articles.text: San Francisco Playhouse is returning to live productions this summer beginning with the premiere of Hold These Truths, which will be performed from June 8 to July 3. Directed by Jeanne Sakata and Jeffrey Lo, Hold These Truths is based on the true story of Gordon Hirabayashi, whose defiance of President Roosevelt’s Executive Order authorizing the incarceration of thousands of Japanese Americans led him to a 50-year journey of advocacy. The play was inspired by many hours of interviews conducted by Sakata with Hirabayashi, as well as primary sources from his life. The New York Times called the play a “gripping story about a shameful chapter of our country’s history,” in its re-telling of the American internment order of 1942. This is the first live production of San Francisco Playhouse since COVID-19 restrictions in March 2020. All COVID guidelines and protocols will be enforced. Book tickets by visiting https://www.sfplayhouse.org/ sfph/upcoming-plays/. Choose seats you’d like and the system will automatically place at least two empty sides on both sides of each group after purchase. Masks must be worn at all times, regardless of vaccination status.

articles.text: A scene from San Francisco Ballet’s production of Helgi Tomasson’s Romeo & Juliet. San Francisco Ballet will stream Helgi Tomasson’s “Romeo & Juliet” through Wednesday, May 26. The multi-capture, cinematic production was performed on-stage at San Francisco’s War Memorial Opera House. The production was the last work that SF Ballet toured prior to 2020 COVID-19 closures. It was performed last in the fall of 2019 at the Royal Danish Opera House in Copenhagen, where it was noted for its “color rich” set design and interpretation of the classic Shakespeare story. The production premiered during SF Ballet’s 1994 Repertory Season and is considered a signature work of the San Francisco Ballet company and has been performed worldwide. Tomasson’s Romeo and Juliet is performed under the direction of SF Ballet music director Martin West, and includes former principal dancers Maria Kochetkova and Davit Karapetyan in the title roles. Pascal Molat, now on faculty at SF Ballet School, is cast as Mercutio. The opulent set is designed by Jens-Jacob Worsaae, with lighting design by Thomas Skelton. This was Worsaae’s final collaboration with Tomasson before he died shortly after the ballet’s premiere. “I think it was the most beautiful work he’d ever done, and yet he did not see it. That’s one reason why this production is very, very special to me,” Tomasson said. To purchase tickets to the streaming production, visit https://www.sfballet.org/productions/digital-program-06/. Swan Lake closes digital season June 9 San Francisco Ballet’s production of Swan Lake is now streaming and will continue through June 9. Tomasson’s Swan Lake will close out the company’s 2021 digital season. The archival performance from 2016 stars Yuan Yuan Tan as Odette-Odile and Tiit Helimets as Prince Siegfried. It features the corps of 30 swans and Odette, whose story is introduced in the prologue. The director showcases male dancers in the first act in his 2009 production. Set and costume designs for the production are by Tony Award-winner Jonathan Fensom. The streaming production is available to watch on-demand until June 9. Visit https://www.sfballet.org/ productions/digital-program-06/ for streaming access. articles.text: George Clooney stars in Up in the Air. For so many reasons Up in the Air is a marvelous movie: stylish, intelligent, poignant and consistently comedic. And yet, beneath its patina of casual elegance and charm is a perpetual tragedy that mirrors the reality of millions of Americans today. The fact that this underlying reality, which is haunting, doesn’t overpower the film is testimony to the brilliance of writer-director Jason Reitman, and a superb acting ensemble led by George Clooney. Clooney portrays Ryan Bingham, a debonair corporate assassin who travels nonstop, from city to city, firing people. It’s a job that the companies themselves are loathe to do. And so he sits across a table and explains to long-time employees that they are being “let go,” as he prefers to say, instead of “fired.” Bingham embraces his life in the air. He has elegantly turned his entrance to and exit from airports into an art form. He packs with studied efficiency, breezes through lines, swipes his cards, flashes his ID and is soon ensconced on the next flight and on his way to the next series of firings. He brags that he spends 322 days on the road and is miserable the other 43 days. He has no home to speak of – his apartment looks like an impersonal hotel room – and no connections to anyone, though he has a sister. He turns the idea of the lonely crowd on its head and his solitary life into an enthusiastic preference absent even a hint of angst. What is so superb about the film is that Bingham is an executioner and the audience is completely beguiled by his smile and intelligence and wit. He never pauses to unpack his emotions or reflect on the impact of his task and for a good part of the film neither does the audience. But then two women enter his life, one a businesswoman, Alex (Vera Farmiga), and Natalie (Melanie Lyskey), a new hire at his company. He meets Alex in a hotel lounge. Natalie is sent on the road with him to learn the ropes, so to speak. Both challenge his view of life, his contented detachment, and his elaborate rationales for his choices. Incrementally, the audience begins to sense that Bingham’s carefully manicured existence may not be as tightly compacted as first assumed. Though the film focuses all but exclusively on Bingham, so likable, so nicely constructed, and perhaps so starkly alone, the real tragedy resides with those he fires. Reitman includes snapshots of non-actors who have been recently let go, asking them to look into the camera and share what it means to lose their jobs after a decade or more. We watch as their faces crumble and they run the gauntlet of emotions. They are the subtext of this film. Up in the Air was one of the best films of 2009, wonderfully written and acted, a quilt of themes, surprising and enjoyable in every way. Up in the Air. Directed by Jason Reitman. Starring George Clooney, Vera Farmiga and Melanie Lynskey. 1 hr., 49 min. Rated R. Vera Farmiga, George Clooney and Melanie Lynskey star in Up in the Air.

articles.text: Captain Fantastic, written and directed by Matt Ross, finds a complex and revelatory sweet spot and expands on it. In so many ways this film is sublimely poetic while remaining firmly grounded as it probes the many facets of what it means to be a parent. It is also an engaging and captivating character study. At the film’s center is Ben, portrayed by Viggo Mortensen, a gifted, nuanced actor who inhabits Ben completely as he grapples with all of the subtle and overt challenges of being a single parent to six very independent children. But their collective lives are not lived in a suburban two-story home somewhere on the west coast; rather, home is a camp or sorts, nestled in the verdant forest of the Pacific Northwest. They live in a place apart, off the grid, and their existence, that of the children, mirrors the values of their father. He strives to instill in them a fearlessness toward life, to think for themselves, to let their minds engage in the seminal questions of purpose and existence, questions that dominate their days and, with the urging of Ben, fill their evenings as they search for answers in books and more books, from literature to philosophy to biology and history; his oldest son, Bodevan (George McKay), has recently decided he is a Maoist, a declaration that prompts a smile from Ben. As well, they are schooled to be survivalists, to engage in extreme rock climbing, hunting, hand-to-hand combat, and they find together a harmony and web of support and concern that so often eludes families surrounded by the trappings and distractions of a consumer-driven pop culture saturated with electronics. What disrupts this harmony is the death of their mother in a hospital in New Mexico where she was taken for treatment. The children, at first devastated, argue strongly, against the wishes of Ben, that they not attend their mother’s funeral. Ben fears the journey could have unintended consequences; however, he finally relents. And suddenly these children of the forest, with all of their attendant skills, are confronted with a culture steeped in all that Ben has attempted to shield them from: television, Gameboy, Walmart and a funeral, organized by their grandparents (Frank Langella and Ann Dowd), a religious ceremony that they know is against the wishes of their mother. This immersion is both humorous and revealing and for most of the children jaw-dropping. These are not feral children, but neither for all of their resilience are they children of this century. Painfully, gradually, Ben is faced with a truth that he has tried to avoid: while his children are supremely prepared for a good part of life, they are also woefully lacking in so many other aspects of what it means to live in a complete world. His didacticism – embedded with his values and convictions and love – has been his gift to them. But the revelation that haunts him is that their lives have been unexpectedly truncated, their prism while wide and encompassing and rich has also been too narrow. Perhaps Ben has loved his children too much. Captain Fantastic is a beautifully crafted film, a story that is life-affirming and lovely, thanks in great part to exceptional writing by Ross and a fine ensemble of actors, all wonderful. Surprisingly, this story comes along at a time when so much of our lives can feel disjointed, and our values seemingly inadequate to the issues that confront us. In essence, our contemporary grid can sometimes seem frayed, at times empty and unfulfilling. And so, Thoreau’s simplicity beckons, the quiet voice that urges us to wander off the grid; it can feel so seductive, the vision/ fantasy seemingly idyllic. But there are larger truths involved than simply leaving the grid. And it is those truths that gradually begin to confront Ben and challenge his vision of the ideal. And it is those truths and their inherent cost that make up the thematic structure of this wonderful film. Captain Fantastic. Starring Viggo Mortensen, Frank Langella and Kathryn Hahn. Directed by Matt Ross. 2 hrs. Rated R.
articles.title: Captain Fantastic a wonderful story of a father and children living off the grid

articles.text: Pixar’s first release with female lead A scene from Pixar’s Brave.. One of Disney’s favorite tropes has been the adorable princess and the wicked stepmother. Recall Snow White and the spiked apple; Cinderella, forced to scrub and clean; or Rapunzel, locked away in a high tower. The movie Brave, directed by Piedmont resident Mark Andrew, does feature a strong-willed teenage princess, Merida (Kelly MacDonald), who rebels not against an unkind stepmother, but against her imperious mother, queen Elinor (Emma Thompson). The period is medieval Scotland, filled with crags and castles and rolling highlands. And there is, of course, Merida, with her massive ginger-colored tresses, a young royal who happens to identify with her father, onelegged, big lug King Fergus (Bill Connoly). She can ride like the wind, and is an expert archer (not unlike Katniss Everdeen of The Hunger Games), and would rather be racing horseback through the surrounding forests than spending time with the staid ladies of the court. Elinor, of course, has her own ideas of how a young princess should behave. But Merida, as wild as her red mane, snorts when she laughs, scoops up food from the pantry, and is a tomboyish, headstrong teenager who has her own ideas regarding gender equality. Queen Elinor is not to be deterred in her efforts to civilize Merida in the image of a domesticated princess, marriage being at the fore. She therefore invites three suitors to the yearly Highland Games, deciding that the best of the three will win her daughter’s hand. Merida, of course, has other plans, finding the three definitely unsuitable as prospective husbands, and defiantly declares to her mother that she’ll not marry, period, followed by an age-appropriate tantrum to make her point. To further drive home her wishes to be her own person, she dominates the archery contest with extraordinary skill and accuracy. But when her mother insists that she will accept the best suitor, Merida runs away into the forest. To her surprise she comes upon a cottage inhabited by an old witch, a crone with magical powers who tells the princess that she can, indeed, cast a spell on Elinor. Merida rashly, rebelliously, agrees. She realizes, too late, however, that her decision has some unintended consequences. In other words, be careful what you wish for when you say, “I want my freedom!” Brave, has more than a few Disneyesque life lessons that result in some tender moments between daughter and mother. This is a wonderfully animated tale that is easy to like. And it’s Pixar’s first female lead out of 13 feature films. Brave. Pixar animation. Directed by Mark Andrews, Brenda Chapman, Steve Purcell. With voices of Kelly MacDonald, Bill Connoly and Emma Thompson, 1 hr., 33 min. A scene from Pixar’s Brave..

articles.text: Abominable, a collaborative animation feature from Dreamworks and China’s Pearl Studios, is, in so many ways, kid-friendly and delightful. So, mom or dad, if you have any youngsters, say newbie tweens, take them to see a film about a spunky-scrappy girl named Yi (Chloe Bennet) who lives in an apartment in Shanghai with her mom (Michelle Wong) and grandmother, Nai Nai (Tsai Chin). Yi, sadly, just lost her dad and has created a small shrine to him on the roof, where she keeps her violin. Alone, after climbing up a precarious scaffolding, she plays solos into the night, music that soars above the city sounds and mournfully expresses her grief. It’s on such an evening that Yi, to her startled and then panicky surprise, discovers that hiding behind a curtain, deep in the shadows, is a young, furry Yeti (the size of a VW bug) with glacially blue eyes. Discovering that this Himalayan creature means her no harm, and seeing an enormous billboard advertising Mt. Everest in the distance, she decides to call him Everest. The audience already knows that Everest has just escaped from a high-tech lab and is now being pursued by a cranky old rich guy, Mr. Burnish (Eddie Lizzard), Dr. Zara (Sarah Paulson), a zoologist, and her mercenary crew. They are intent on recapturing Everest. And so begins a great adventure. Yi, realizing where this Yeti must have come from, decides he must be returned to his home and his family. She recruits two long-time friends who live in her building – Jin (Tenzing Norgay Trainor), a classmate, and Peng, who is obsessed with basketball. Together they head out with Everest on a road trip (to include river barges) making their way toward Mt. Everest. Of course, Burnish, Zara, and company are in hot pursuit, prepared to do whatever it takes to get Everest back to the Shanghai lab, for reasons never fully explained. As expected, while they travel cross-country, the crew have lots of close calls, keeping just barely ahead of the bad guys. Along the way there are also lyrical moments when Yi plays her muchloved violin. And there are those moments when the gang discovers that Everest isn’t just a Yeti but possesses magical powers that he calls forth when needed. In one beautiful scene, running from Burnish and Zara, Everest turns a field of flowers into an undulating cresting wave that they surf while riding in a small wooden boat, surrounded by a riot of pastel colors. It’s superb animation, filled with breathtaking imagination. What is done so well in Abominable is that the writers and animators nail not only the wonderful pastel panoramas, but they create, in Yi and Jin and Jeng, kids that seem truly authentic. Yi has just the right amount of courage and attitude. Jin is a perfect newbie teen who, like Yi, is goodhearted and kind. Peng is about the same age as Everest (ten, perhaps?), and they form a bro-bond that is always resilient and fun to watch. All of them are there not only for Everest, but committed to each other as they meet challenge after challenge on their way to getting Everest home. Of course, they learn some nifty life lessons along the way, especially about family and friendship. Is Abominable formulaic? Indeed. But in the best sense of the word. Does it have a right ending? Indeed. Kids dig stories that are accessible and comfortable and familiar with easydoes-it excitement. This movie gets all of that just right. So, mom and dad, no worries. Abominable . Animated. Voices of Chloe Bennet, Albert Tai, Tenzing Norgay Trainor. 1 hr., 37 min. Rated PG.
articles.title: Abominable a lovely animation feature that gets it right

articles.text: Violinist Grisha Goluboff (left) with Henry Ford in the 1930s. Grisha Goluboff is the forgotten genius of the violin. The city of San Francisco in the 20th century can boast of four of the greatest violinists of all time. Three made it to everlasting fame. You know their names. articles.text: Brown Gables, the Alexander home at Sea View and Hampton, was named for its prominent gables, painted brown. Their grand three-story mansion was completed in 1909, and they named it “Brown Gables” for its massive gabled dormers with bargeboards, painted brown. The first floor was faced in brick, and half timbering covered the upper stories. Two large porte cocheres were also trimmed in brown gables. Diamond paned leaded glass windows graced the entry, and large bay windows offered expansive views from every room in this most elegant early home in Piedmont. City records indicate that the Alexander house had three living rooms, five bedrooms and five bathrooms. Koa wood and other exotic woods enhanced the interior. It was an exceptional house in 1909 with 3240 square feet, and was the site of many festive balls. The gardens of the Alexander home also hosted many garden parties benefiting local charities. Mary Alexander was a strong supporter of the Ladies Relief Society, the Matilda Brown Home and the Women’s Guild of the Piedmont Church. She also organized the Bay Area chapter of the Red Cross at the onset of World War I and led it for over 30 years. Their beautiful gardens extended over nine of today’s lots on Sea View and King Avenues. A low brick wall with a subtle detail surrounded the property. The wall is visible in the photo of the house, and portions still stand today on Hampton. The Alexander carriage house, which still exists at 84 King, had servants’ quarters and an indoor swimming pool. Helen Wills Moody, the Wimbledon tennis star in the 1920s and 1930s, practiced on the tennis court there. The Alexander family formed a small community near Sea View and Hampton. In 1911, Wallace’s mother built her own home across the street at 92 Sea View, designed by Charles W. Dickey, and Mary’s mother built her home down the street at 236 Sea View. Wallace Alexander was president of the Alexander and Baldwin sugar firm, vice president of the Matson Navigation Company, director of several other Hawaiian companies and a trustee of Stanford University. Although he was active in many businesses, he found time for many civic and charitable organizations in Piedmont. In addition to constructing the stores and saving Piedmont Park, Alexander was also the moving force behind the construction of the Piedmont Interdenominational Church (now Piedmont Community Church), arranging for the purchase of the land and again hiring Albert Farr to design the church. Wallace Alexander also established the Piedmont Boy Scout Council. He arranged for the scouts to meet in the basement of the church, as they still do today. In 1929, he leased land from the Forest Service near Keddie, in Plumas County, and established Camp Wallace Alexander, a Piedmont scouting tradition fondly remembered by generations of Piedmont Boy Scouts. The land lease expired in 1982, and Camp Wallace Alexander was dismantled. In 1939, Wallace Alexander suffered a fatal stroke at his second home in Honolulu. He was eulogized as “Piedmont’s leading private citizen.” Wallace left a large bequest to the Piedmont Community Church and to the Piedmont Boy Scouts. His philosophy was that he “was but a trustee of the money that came to him.” Upon his death, Mary Alexander followed her husband’s wishes that the property be subdivided into 13 lots. The entire estate would not be sold to a single builder. She stated that the lots would be purchased by individuals who intended to build their own homes. The Alexanders wanted more families to live in Piedmont. Footnote on the Stores My previous column on Piedmont’s “stores” brought out a few comments by readers. articles.text: Wallace Alexander was Piedmont’s premier philanthropic citizen and a leader in establishing many of Piedmont’s institutions. In previous columns I have mentioned Wallace Alexander. He was instrumental in the 1913 construction of the Piedmont Commercial Center, Piedmont’s first stores, and in the 1921 purchase of the upper Piedmont Park land, saving it from development. Wallace Alexander, a profile Wallace McKinney Alexander was born on the island of Maui in 1869. His father, Samuel Alexander, was related to the Baldwin and Cooke families and was a pioneer in sugar planting and refining. When it was time for Wallace and his sisters, Juliette and Annie, to attend high school, the family moved to Oakland where Wallace attended Oakland High School. He later attended Andover and graduated from Yale University. He married Oakland classmate Mary Barker in 1904. In her memoir, Queen of the Hills, Evelyn Craig Pattiani tells the story of the Alexanders choosing their homesite at the prominent corner of Sea View and Hampton (then called Union Street). articles.text: In addition to the more prominent architectural styles we have been discussing during the last months, there are yet more to be seen walking through town. Some, like Victorian, are well known but not numerous here; others are hybrid, sometimes difficult to classify. But it also strikes me that every new building, or even every remodel, is necessarily advancing, albeit in small steps, the evolution of any and every base style employed. Looking back maybe 50 years from now, these incremental trends will probably be clearer and help describe how and why the future style came to be. To better understand the initial selection and continuing evolution of building styles it might be helpful to review the process architects normally employ in design. Based on my experience, there are three overriding considerations in the design of any building: the site, the building program, and the design style. 1. Any building site has a specific size, solar orientation, topography, along with existing amenities (like views, trees, rock outcroppings, or water features for example). Any site is also a part of a surrounding context – anything from vacant land to 2-story homes to 12-story office buildings. 2. The building program answers the questions: how big is the intended building? What types of uses and spaces are included? What service systems are included? While zoning regulations limit these options, there still are a wide range of choices based on user lifestyle preference, cost, and response to the site. 3. The design style chosen, no matter how closely or loosely followed, determines the aesthetic of both the building massing and details – inside and out. It influences materials, forms and siting. While the two long continuous slender columned porches on both levels suggest Monterey Colonial style architecture, this house ends up principally as a backdrop for the incredible front garden and brickwork. It is the kind of special personalized property that makes Piedmont wonderful.

articles.text: Back in the pre-Covid days when they actually had big, live wine tasting events, one of the perennial favorites was the Rhone Rangers tasting. It was held at varied venues in the Bay Area and featured about 100 wineries who specialize in Rhone grape varietals grown in California. They were raucous events filled with passionate wine producers and wine lovers. Every year when it came to selecting the 10 best wines of the tasting, Austin Hope always ended among the winners, whether it was their Grenache, Syrah or one of their blends. The Hope Family has been farming in Paso Robles for 30 years, getting their start with apple orchards. Today they have expanded to five brands – Austin Hope, Treana, Quest, Liberty School, and Troublemaker. I recently was able to taste the current releases of the Austin Hope wines and get caught up on how the winery is doing today. • 2020 Austin Hope Chenin Blanc There used to be a lot of Chenin Blanc planted in California, but much of it was converted to Cabernet or Chardonnay vineyards. Luckily a resurgence seems to be afoot as it truly is one of the finest white grapes on the planet. The Austin Hope Chenin Blanc is a brilliantly focused, vibrant, fresh and delicious dry wine that is bursting with fruit and seductive, flowery aromas. Crisp and fragrant, it is hard to imagine a better aperitif than a wine such as this. • 2019 Austin Hope Sauvignon Blanc The Hope Sauvignon Blanc has expressive green apple and fresh grass notes with hints of jasmine, lime and grapefruit. Medium-bodied, the palate has tons of freshness with loads of citrusy layers and a smooth, clean finish. Would be great with fish or shellfish. • 2019 Austin Hope Chardonnay This Chardonnay opens with notes of almonds, hay, and peach with nuances of yeast, bread and flowers. Medium-bodied, it fleshes out in the mouth to tropical-tinged fruits, with juicy freshness on the finish. Try with roast chicken. • 2020 Austin Hope Rose This is one of the lightest colored Roses I have seen, with just a glimmer of copper coloring. It has a nose of strawberries, currant jelly and baking spices plus a waft of dried herbs. The palate is medium-bodied with a wonderful freshness lifting the spicy berry flavors, finishing clean and crisp. • 2019 Austin Hope Mourvedre/Syrah This 50/50 blende of two of the Rhone Valleys most important grapes is one of the first wines I had from Austin Hope and is representative of their style. The rich nose of blueberry, and Blend of Syrah and Mourvedre from Austin Hope. plum fruit mixed with earth and leather jumps from the glass. In the mouth there is an explosion of dense, juicy, mouth filling berry fruit but with good structure and definition. The finish is long and satisfying. • 2019 Austin Hope Cabernet Franc I have never been a fan of the Cab Francs from France – especially the Loire Valley. They are often green, vegetal and underripe. But the grape seems to thrive in sunny, hot Paso Robles and this is a good example. It has a vibrant nose of currants and cherries with touches of cedar and violets. Medium bodied and elegantly played on the palate, it has a solid structure of chewy tannins and lively acid supporting the juicy berry flavors, finishing long with some earth notes coming through. The perfect partner for a grilled ribeye steak. • 2019 Austin Hope Lagrein & Petite Sirah (50/50) I was totally excited to try this absolutely unique blend. Lagrein is a rare, elegant grape from the extreme north of Italy where it grows in the foothills of the Alps, and Petite Sirah is…. well you know, the Muhammad Ali of red grapes. So what do you get when you put these odd fellows together? Very deep purple-black colored wine, the nose shows roses, violets, ripe plums and blackberries with touches of tilled soil and dried herbs. Very full-bodied, the palate is superfirm and chewy, yet the tannins are nice and ripe, framing the black fruits beautifully, finishing long and chewy. An outstanding unique wine. Try with a hearty beef or lamb stew. Austin Hope’s unique blend of Lagrein and Petite Sirah.

pages.text: Wednesday, May 19, 2021 23 The Wine Corner Austin Hope Wines By Pierre DuMont Back in the pre-Covid days when they actually had big, live wine tasting events, one of the perennial favorites was the Rhone Rangers tasting. It was held at varied venues in the Bay Area and featured about 100 wineries who specialize in Rhone grape varietals grown in California. They were raucous events filled with passionate wine producers and wine lovers. Every year when it came to selecting the 10 best wines of the tasting, Austin Hope always ended among the winners, whether it was their Grenache, Syrah or one of their blends. The Hope Family has been farming in Paso Robles for 30 years, getting their start with apple orchards. Today they have expanded to five brands – Austin Hope, Treana, Quest, Liberty School, and Troublemaker. I recently was able to taste the current releases of the Austin Hope wines and get caught up on how the winery is doing today. • 2020 Austin Hope Chenin Blanc There used to be a lot of Chenin Blanc planted in California, but much of it was converted to Cabernet or Chardonnay vineyards. Luckily a resurgence seems to be afoot as it truly is one of the finest white grapes on the planet. The Austin Hope Chenin Blanc is a brilliantly focused, vibrant, fresh and delicious dry wine that is bursting with fruit and seductive, flowery aromas. Crisp and fragrant, it is hard to imagine a better aperitif than a wine such as this. • 2019 Austin Hope Sauvignon Blanc The Hope Sauvignon Blanc has expressive green apple and fresh grass notes with hints of jasmine, lime and grapefruit. Medium-bodied, the palate has tons of freshness with loads of citrusy layers and a smooth, clean finish. Would be great with fish or shellfish. • 2019 Austin Hope Chardonnay This Chardonnay opens with notes of almonds, hay, and peach with nuances of yeast, bread and flowers. Medium-bodied, it fleshes out in the mouth to tropical-tinged fruits, with juicy freshness on the finish. Try with roast chicken. • 2020 Austin Hope Rose This is one of the lightest colored Roses I have seen, with just a glimmer of copper coloring. It has a nose of strawberries, currant jelly and baking spices plus a waft of dried herbs. The palate is medium-bodied with a wonderful freshness lifting the spicy berry flavors, finishing clean and crisp. • 2019 Austin Hope Mourvedre/Syrah This 50/50 blende of two of the Rhone Valleys most important grapes is one of the first wines I had from Austin Hope and is representative of their style. The rich nose of blueberry, and Blend of Syrah and Mourvedre from Austin Hope. plum fruit mixed with earth and leather jumps from the glass. In the mouth there is an explosion of dense, juicy, mouth filling berry fruit but with good structure and definition. The finish is long and satisfying. • 2019 Austin Hope Cabernet Franc I have never been a fan of the Cab Francs from France – especially the Loire Valley. They are often green, vegetal and underripe. But the grape seems to thrive in sunny, hot Paso Robles and this is a good example. It has a vibrant nose of currants and cherries with touches of cedar and violets. Medium bodied and elegantly played on the palate, it has a solid structure of chewy tannins and lively acid supporting the juicy berry flavors, finishing long with some earth notes coming through. The perfect partner for a grilled ribeye steak. • 2019 Austin Hope Lagrein & Petite Sirah (50/50) I was totally excited to try this absolutely unique blend. Lagrein is a rare, elegant grape from the extreme north of Italy where it grows in the foothills of the Alps, and Petite Sirah is…. well you know, the Muhammad Ali of red grapes. So what do you get when you put these odd fellows together? Very deep purple-black colored wine, the nose shows roses, violets, ripe plums and blackberries with touches of tilled soil and dried herbs. Very full-bodied, the palate is superfirm and chewy, yet the tannins are nice and ripe, framing the black fruits beautifully, finishing long and chewy. An outstanding unique wine. Try with a hearty beef or lamb stew. Austin Hope’s unique blend of Lagrein and Petite Sirah. articles.text: Photo by Katie Heatherington The Recreation Department-sponsored Walking on Wednesday group visited Hampton Park last week. Pictured are Harriette Louie (left), Nancy DeRoche and k-9 best friend Chili, Jim Kuo, Brenda Ferrero, Melba Yee and Albert Chen. Not pictured Andree and Mark Greenberg, and Susan Martin. The sun broke through the morning fog just as the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group departed from the Exedra for its walk on May 12th. Ten walkers were on hand: Harriette Louie, Brenda Ferrero, Jim Kuo, Adrienne Hamlin, Susan Martin, Albert Chen, Andree Greenberg, Mark Greenberg, Nancy DeRoche and Melba Yee. Since the group resumed its activities after the pandemic put them on hold for one year, the walkers have been visiting some of the area’s wonderful parks and recreational facilities. They have gone to Dracena Park, the Davie Tennis Stadium, and the Morcom Rose Garden. On May 12 it was decided that going to Piedmont’s Hampton Park with its Piedmont Sports Field, also as known as Hampton Field, would add to their park-seeing collection. Activity leader Dick Carter was out of town, so Harriette Louie and Melba Yee stepped in to lead the day’s walk. The walkers went up Highland Avenue to Sheridan Avenue, then to Wildwood Avenue, and through the Hall Fenway to Crocker and Hampton Avenues. They took a short side trip to Crocker Park to enjoy its flowers and the sculpture Mother Bear Nursing Her Two Cubs by noted San Francisco-base sculptor Beniamino “Benny” Bufano. It was gifted to the city and installed in Crocker Park in 1979. It is described by the City as granite, but described by the Smithsonian American Art Museum as black marble. The walkers closely examined the sculpture and all agreed the material was indeed granite. Three other copies of the Bear and Cubs sculpture, rendered in different materials, can be found outside the Oakland Museum, the Kaiser Hospital in Fremont, and near UC San Francisco. Crocker Park was gifted to the city in 1916 by Mary and Wallace Alexander, owners of a large home that covered the entire block between Crocker and Sea View Avenues. In addition to being one of the city’s founding fathers, Wallace Alexander’s civic contributions to the city were significant and enduring: he founded the Piedmont Boy Scouts in 1910; helped the city buy Piedmont Springs Park from Frank Havens; led a group of residents to purchase 2 acres of land across from Piedmont Park. He hired Albert Farr to design the town’s commercial center, and later to design the Piedmont Community Church. Despite his many contributions, most of the walkers had not heard of Wallace Alexander and the group wondered whether any honorary designations existed in town. The sole surviving structure from the Alexander estate is a residence across the street from the park on Crocker Avenue. Nancy DeRoche informed the group that this structure was originally the carriage house, and that it is probably representative of the architectural style of the now-destroyed main house. The group then left the park and went up Hampton past a set of huge eucalyptus trees where St. James Drive ends at Hampton. They continued up the street to Hampton Park. Hampton Park has evolved greatly over the years. Drawing on information from Piedmont Historical Society President Gail Lombardi’s research, the walkers learned that Hampton Park was part of 50 acres purchased in 1911 by Louis Titus, a Berkeley real estate developer. He intended to build a mansion on this large tract of land, but in 1912 the new city of Piedmont raised property taxes significantly, and Titus dropped his plans and left Piedmont. In 1914 James Tyson, a lumber and shipping businessman bought 30 acres of the land for his home. Tyson was also a strong supporter of Piedmont Boy Scouts, and in 1921 Tyson made a portion of the land available for the scouts to use as an outdoor camp. During the Great Depression in 1938 the Tysons also make the land available to the Piedmont schools. A WPA project leveled the land and it was intended to be the site of a future “East Piedmont” school. However, it was never built. In the 50s and 60s the space was a dusty, sometimes muddy baseball field for younger players. Later, when grass was planted on the field, youth soccer matches were played, sometimes on a soggy field. An underground water flow was an on-going problem. Hampton Park and the Piedmont Sports Field are much different today than what Piedmonters experienced 100, 50, and even 20 years ago. A building was constructed in 2000 to house children’s programs that is used by both the Piedmont Cooperative Playschool and the Recreation Department. Dramatic improvements were made to the field and park during 2017 with a $2 million public/private partnership that the Piedmont community generously supported. Drainage and artificial turf were installed that made the field much more serviceable during the year. In 2019 the baseball backstop was dedicated and named in honor of Oakland Police Officer John Raymond Hege. The 41-year-old Piedmont native was one of four officers fatally shot following a traffic stop in East Oakland on March 21, 2009. The field is used today for organized baseball, soccer and children’s activities. The park also has two tennis courts, a backboard, a volleyball court, and six basketball hoops. There is a children’s play structure and sand area that are located near the tennis courts.

articles.text: Mollie Kinney, a longtime Piedmont resident, died peacefully in her sleep on the evening of April 20, 2021 after a long illness, with her husband by her side. Born Marie Mitchell Mulford, she was the oldest daughter of Lloyd and Adele Mulford of Piedmont. She was born in Oakland, and attended schools in Piedmont, graduating from Piedmont High school in 1949. She earned a degree from Nursing School at St. Francis Hospital in San Francisco, and though a nurse all of her life, she never practiced nursing. During her time in nurses training, she established many lasting friendships and enjoyed immensely their yearly reunions. Everyone who knew Mollie remembers her laugh, and her wonderful, positive view of life. She could look at everything with humor. Not only that but she could always sneak in a good nap. Mollie met her husband, Bill Kinney, when he was in the milMollie Kinney with her favorite cup of coffee. “Aloha” from the Islands. Mollie and Bill Kinney in Hawaii – “Five o’clock in Paradise.” itary during the Korean conflict. They corresponded for the two years and when he returned, they were married at St. Paul’s Church in Oakland on September 26, 1953. They lived in the country for a short time before moving to Piedmont, where Mollie lived the rest of her life. Mollie was a member of the Piedmont Garden Club, Hoe and Hope Garden Club, and the Piedmont Beautification Foundation. She was also a member of the Junior League of the East Bay and a longtime member of Claremont Country Club where she enjoyed playing golf, tennis and bridge. She most often could be found playing bridge somewhere. She loved the game and the friends she made playing over the years. She was also a wonderful athlete. She spent the early years of her life riding and jumping horses. When that career ended, she took up golf and tennis and was excellent at both. Additionally, she loved dogs, especially Springer Spaniels. Mollie loved spending time with her many friends, gardening, and playing bridge, and attending sporting events especially if her children or grandchildren were playing. Most of all, she loved her family and spent quality time with friends and family members at home, at Claremont, on vacation trips, or at the family cabin on the American River near Kyburz. Mollie Kinney is survived by William A. Kinney, her husband of 68 years, and her two sons, Bill Kinney, Jr. and his wife Susie of Las Vegas, and Jim Kinney and his wife Geanne of Alameda. She is also survived by four grandchildren, Becky and Jeffrey Kinney of Las Vegas, Caroline and Kevin Kinney of Alameda, and by two great grandsons, Cooper and Barrett Kinney. Mollie is also survived by “little” sister Susie McPhee and husband Sandy and their children Chip (Ali), Mollie (Pat), and Robbie (Jody), and seven grandchildren, Kelly and Charlie McPhee (Chip and Ali), Katie, Abigail and Jake Callahan, and Jordan and Rachael McPhee. Mollie will be greatly missed by her entire family and all who knew her. A small family gathering will be held in Mollie’s memory at a future date. In lieu of flowers, the family suggests that memorial donations may be made to the Piedmont Beautification Foundation, c/o Piedmont City Hall, 120 Vista Avenue, Piedmont, California 94611.
