articles.text: Sociologists have a term to describe a contemporary family dynamic that has been the norm in many cultures for centuries: intensive grandparenting. Today’s intensive grandparents provide weekly, regular childcare for grandchildren, as well as providing additional support such as housework, shopping for groceries, carpooling, and preparing meals. These care arrangements may begin with full-time care of an infant when the mother returns to work and may continue as the child ages to include after-school care and coverage for sick days. As author Paula Span writes in her NY Times article for Generation Grandparent, “When grandparents help hold it all together,” intensive grandparents are not necessarily defined by the number of hours per week they provide care, but rather by their commitment to the task longterm. It allows working parents the opportunity to rely on the grandparents in the same way they would a hired caregiver. For grandmothers in particular, there can be a strong motivation to help their adult children in this way, even when those grandmothers are still working. These working grandmothers treasure time with their grandchildren, and yet they may find themselves tapping into their employee benefits and retirement accounts prematurely. Many have aging parents to care for as well, so that being an intensive grandparent can lead to lost personal time and some of their own social support system. When grandparents embark on this kind of arrangement voluntarily, the results can be delightful. Grandparents who live close by and who are physically fit enough to provide regular childcare can make lifelong memories with their grandchildren. The rewards can be extraordinary. Many discover pleasures that they may have missed out on when they were raising their own children, and these joys can be unlike any other that they’ve experienced. One Korean study found that intensive grandchild care compared to grandparents who provide no grandchild care is associated with a reduction in depressive symptoms in older adults, particularly men. Intensive grandparenting may have different outcomes in other situations. A study in Ireland found that the emotional effects of intensive caring on grandparents is strongly affected by whether the care is provided by choice or by obligation. In families where the care is requested due to socioeconomic constraints, the grandparents may find it nearly impossible to say No. In this study, grandparents who provide high intensity care showed an increase in depressive symptoms and a decrease in their sense of well-being, particularly if they did not have a balance of social and leisure activity in their lives. Each family that employs an intensive grandparenting plan is unique, and the factors that motivate these arrangements can be vastly different across households. Social norms and national public policy initiatives relating to affordable childcare are a work in progress and one day may change the face of grandparent care. Meanwhile, if you are an intensive grandparent, consider how to make the most of your time with your family and find balance for yourself as well. articles.text: It might be time to start thinking about being together again. Well-being is not just about exercise and nutrition, but also relationships and emotional resilience. Beyond spending time with immediate family, studies have found that people can benefit from all kinds of relationships in their lives. A decades-long Harvard University study found that close relationships spanning a lifetime can alleviate pain levels, support the nervous system, and keep the brain healthier longer. On the other hand, those who feel a prolonged sense of loneliness may have a shorter lifespan. Here are some ways to prioritize togetherness and relationships to benefit not only you but also those in your life whom you care about. 1. Make time It’s so easy to get caught up in daily tasks, the ‘to-do’ list and the ‘should ofs’ in life. “It’s easy to get isolated,” said Professor Robert Waldinger, director of the Harvard Study of Adult Development, in an interview. He suggests “investing time in relationships”. 2. Be casual Keeping up relationships isn’t about the big events of life, but the little moments. If you can get together in-person in a way that feels safe for all parties, then go out and do something meaningful together. In instances where you cannot be in the same place, send a card just because, call them up to share a story, or find a way to connect online through a shared game or activity. 3. Move past the shame of loneliness. People often feel ashamed of their feelings of loneliness. It can feel like admitting you are lonely is akin to saying you are not likeable; that you are socially deficient in some way. This feeling is actually an instinctual survival skill and is perfectly natural. But at the same time, loneliness can have negative physical consequences. Rather than being ashamed, recognize loneliness as the body signaling a biological need, just like hunger or thirst. 4. Know that age doesn’t matter. Experts agree that human connection and togetherness is important at every age and people of different ages can have essential relationships. People can make new friends throughout life by sharing a hobby, activity, or story. Beyond grandparents and grandchildren, friendships can develop across an age gap through a caregiving connection, in a work environment, or by engaging in shared interests. 5. You go first. Stop waiting for the phone to ring. If that feeling of loneliness is nagging at you, be the one to take the initiative. Try getting in touch with an old friend or make new ones by joining an in-person or online group. There are book clubs, caregiver support groups, knitting circles, and much more out there to become part of. articles.text: After a year of being cooped up, everyone I know is delighted with this beautiful spring weather we are having. Many of us are going outside and are so happy to increase our activity level to regain physical fitness. Yet, one of the discoveries we’ve made in a year of staying indoors is that there are ways to develop our inner strength and resiliency. One very popular way we’ve found to restore ourselves in the face of the unpredictable, and to enrich both the mind and soul, is through meditation and mindfulness exercises. Residents of The Lake Merritt - Independent Senior Living community have found this to be true. Many have been practicing mindfulness exercises for years. Meghan Collins, a resident since 2012, has been a Zen practitioner for 45 years and a lay teacher for 22 years. She has been leading our meditation group since she moved to The Lake Merritt. “The residents tell me it is very calming and beneficial,” Collins says. Medical professionals concur. According to the National Institute of Health, there is a beneficial link between mindfulness meditation and measurable changes in the brain regions involved in memory, learning and emotion. Data indicates that meditation can also help improve psychological balance, coping with illness, and may enhance overall health and well-being. The Lake Merritt’s yoga instructor, Bethany Hobbs, couldn’t agree more. She offers classes of Chair Yoga, Meditation & Relaxation, and Balance Awareness for our community. Her work focuses on breathing, balance, stretching and strengthening the body, as well as the Wes Nisker and Megan Collins and lead a meditation session at The Lake Merritt in Oakland. mind, so that older adults can help keep both their minds and bodies more flexible and relaxed. The Lake Merritt’s newest resident, Wes Nisker, is a Buddhist meditation teacher, author, and performer. His books include national bestseller, Essential Crazy Wisdom, as well as Buddha’s Nature and The Big Bang, The Buddha, and the Baby Boom. Nisker has studied Buddhist meditation for over three decades with teachers in Asia and America. For the past 15 years he has been leading retreats and workshops in Buddhist insight meditation and philosophy at national and international venues. Collins and Nisker were excited to meet one another and have recently joined forces in leading the meditation group at The Lake Merritt. When asked whether they prefer to lead or participate, they are in agreement. “When you lead you are trying to experience what you are calling on others to do. You don’t let go as deeply into the experience,” says Nisker. “As a participant, you can just let go. When you lead. you have to keep track of the time and things around you. Over the years I’ve learned to do both,” adds Collins. A major benefit of mindfulness meditation is that it encourages you to pay attention to your thoughts, your actions and your body. Finding time for mindfulness in our culture, however, can be a challenge. We tend to place great value on how much we can do at once and how fast. Being more mindful is within anyone’s reach. “Over the years it seems the practice of meditation has given me a lot more equilibrium,” Collins says. Given the very turbulent times we have been through recently, it seems like meditation might be just the thing for everyone. Tim Johnson is Executive Director of The Lake Merritt - Independent Senior Living, 1800 Madison Street, Oakland. For more information call 510-903- 3600 or visit www.thelakemerritt. com.

articles.text: On May 21, Stagebridge and Asian American Storytellers in Unity will join forces to uplift the diverse cultures and heritage of the Asian American and Pacific Islander diaspora in Finding Ourselves in America: Asian American Voices. pages.text: Wednesday, May 19, 2021 29 Meditation: Food for the mind and soul By Tim Johnson After a year of being cooped up, everyone I know is delighted with this beautiful spring weather we are having. Many of us are going outside and are so happy to increase our activity level to regain physical fitness. Yet, one of the discoveries we’ve made in a year of staying indoors is that there are ways to develop our inner strength and resiliency. One very popular way we’ve found to restore ourselves in the face of the unpredictable, and to enrich both the mind and soul, is through meditation and mindfulness exercises. Residents of The Lake Merritt - Independent Senior Living community have found this to be true. Many have been practicing mindfulness exercises for years. Meghan Collins, a resident since 2012, has been a Zen practitioner for 45 years and a lay teacher for 22 years. She has been leading our meditation group since she moved to The Lake Merritt. “The residents tell me it is very calming and beneficial,” Collins says. Medical professionals concur. According to the National Institute of Health, there is a beneficial link between mindfulness meditation and measurable changes in the brain regions involved in memory, learning and emotion. Data indicates that meditation can also help improve psychological balance, coping with illness, and may enhance overall health and well-being. The Lake Merritt’s yoga instructor, Bethany Hobbs, couldn’t agree more. She offers classes of Chair Yoga, Meditation & Relaxation, and Balance Awareness for our community. Her work focuses on breathing, balance, stretching and strengthening the body, as well as the Wes Nisker and Megan Collins and lead a meditation session at The Lake Merritt in Oakland. mind, so that older adults can help keep both their minds and bodies more flexible and relaxed. The Lake Merritt’s newest resident, Wes Nisker, is a Buddhist meditation teacher, author, and performer. His books include national bestseller, Essential Crazy Wisdom, as well as Buddha’s Nature and The Big Bang, The Buddha, and the Baby Boom. Nisker has studied Buddhist meditation for over three decades with teachers in Asia and America. For the past 15 years he has been leading retreats and workshops in Buddhist insight meditation and philosophy at national and international venues. Collins and Nisker were excited to meet one another and have recently joined forces in leading the meditation group at The Lake Merritt. When asked whether they prefer to lead or participate, they are in agreement. “When you lead you are trying to experience what you are calling on others to do. You don’t let go as deeply into the experience,” says Nisker. “As a participant, you can just let go. When you lead. you have to keep track of the time and things around you. Over the years I’ve learned to do both,” adds Collins. A major benefit of mindfulness meditation is that it encourages you to pay attention to your thoughts, your actions and your body. Finding time for mindfulness in our culture, however, can be a challenge. We tend to place great value on how much we can do at once and how fast. Being more mindful is within anyone’s reach. “Over the years it seems the practice of meditation has given me a lot more equilibrium,” Collins says. Given the very turbulent times we have been through recently, it seems like meditation might be just the thing for everyone. articles.text: An intelligent response to and prioritization of each of these overlapping and integrated considerations is what makes for successful architecture. What is occurring over time, however, is that each and every one of these three important considerations is in flux – they are always changing. Adjacent trees grow, neighboring buildings are built, and overhead utility lines are removed. Just accommodating current lifestyles, newer building methods, and improved material selections necessarily changes and advances any base architectural style initially chosen with every year that passes. A partial exception to this would be the case of strict historical renovations where exact themes and details are duplicated for historical accuracy. So, it is easy to see how all architectural styles can evolve. And with changes in the world occurring more rapidly, the style evolutions will also occur faster. Just think of the pandemic we are now in. More time spent in the house with virtual activities has created in one year a whole new set of building program criteria to which architects, designers, engineers, and their clients are already responding.
